options.text: The rate of unauthorised or out-of-policy actions, such as refunds initiated without the required conditions, across test scenarios.
options.explanation: Correct. For an agent that acts, the key safety outcome is whether it ever takes an action that it should not.

questions.taskStatement: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
questions.stem:
An architect is three weeks from the planned launch of a customer-facing assistant when the security team first hears of the project. Security requires a threat model and a penetration test, and legal requires a review of the data-processing terms. The launch is delayed by two months. The project's discovery phase had involved only the product owner and two engineers.

What should the architect do differently in future projects?

options.text: Identify every stakeholder with approval rights during discovery, and gather their requirements and review timelines at the start.
options.explanation: Correct. Structured discovery includes stakeholder identification. Requirements from approval functions that arrive late cause rework and delay.

options.text: Ask the product owner to sign a statement accepting all security and legal risk.
options.explanation: The product owner generally has no authority to waive these reviews, and the risks remain unassessed.

options.text: Keep security and legal out of projects until a working system exists for them to review after launch, to protect delivery dates and avoid speculative objections.
options.explanation: This does not remove their requirements. It moves the discovery of them to the most expensive moment.

options.text: Add a standard two-month buffer to every project plan.
options.explanation: A buffer absorbs the delay without capturing the requirements early, when they could shape the design.

questions.taskStatement: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
questions.stem:
A logistics company asks for an AI system to "improve the accuracy of customs classification". During discovery the architect learns that nobody has measured current accuracy, that there are no labelled examples of correct classifications, and that two senior classifiers disagree on what the correct code is for some goods.

What should happen before the solution is designed?

options.text: Promise 99% accuracy in the proposal, to set an ambitious target.
options.explanation: A target without a measured baseline or agreed ground truth cannot be justified or verified.

options.text: Use the more senior classifier's codes as ground truth, and design the system to match them.
options.explanation: Choosing one expert's view without resolving the disagreement bakes an unexamined definition of 'correct' into the target, and still leaves no measured baseline.

options.text: Establish a baseline: have experts label a representative sample, resolve their disagreements, and agree acceptance criteria.
options.explanation: Correct. Improvement cannot be demonstrated without a baseline and an agreed definition of correct. Discovery has to produce both.

options.text: Skip measurement of the current process, on the assumption that the model will be more accurate than people who cannot agree among themselves.
options.explanation: The experts themselves disagree on ground truth. The assumption cannot be tested without doing the work.

questions.taskStatement: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
questions.stem:
An internal policy assistant is given retrieved policy excerpts with each question. When the excerpts do not cover the question, it answers from general knowledge in an authoritative tone, and employees have acted on advice that contradicts company policy. The requirement is that answers reflect company policy only, with a clear signal when policy does not cover the question.

Which guardrail should be added to the system prompt?

options.text: An instruction to prefer the excerpts over general knowledge, and to use general knowledge only to fill gaps the excerpts leave.
options.explanation: This still allows ungrounded answers whenever the excerpts are silent, which is exactly the failure the requirement forbids.

options.text: An instruction to answer only from the provided excerpts, to cite the excerpt used, and to say explicitly when the excerpts do not contain the answer, pointing the employee to the policy team.
options.explanation: Correct. A grounding instruction with an explicit, acceptable way to say that the answer is not available stops the model from filling gaps with general knowledge.

options.text: An instruction to add "this may not be correct" to every answer.
options.explanation: A blanket disclaimer does not separate grounded answers from ungrounded ones, and employees will learn to ignore it.

options.text: An instruction to "be as accurate as possible".
options.explanation: The model already believes its general-knowledge answers are accurate. This does not restrict the source.

questions.taskStatement: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
questions.stem:
A pharmacy group runs an overnight job that checks every new prescription against the patient's current medication for dangerous interactions. Results are needed by 6 a.m., which leaves about 30 seconds per prescription. A single model call takes 4 seconds and detects 93% of the known interactions in the test set. Adding an independent verification call that re-examines the result against the interaction reference raises detection to 98% and takes 11 seconds in total. A missed interaction can harm a patient.

Which configuration is justified?

options.text: The single call, with the smallest model, to finish the job as early as possible.
options.explanation: Finishing early has no stated benefit, and an untested smaller model could lower detection further.

options.text: The configuration with the verification call, because the time budget accommodates it easily and the gain in accuracy matters greatly for safety.
options.explanation: Correct. Accuracy-latency trade-offs depend on context. Here latency has ample headroom and errors are very costly, so the slower, more accurate configuration is the right choice.

options.text: The single call, because it is almost three times faster.
options.explanation: The speed has no value when 30 seconds are available, and it leaves 5 points of detection unused in a safety-critical task.

options.text: Neither. Interaction checking should run in real time during the day.
options.explanation: The requirement is an overnight batch with results by 6 a.m. Moving it to real time changes the problem and removes the latency headroom.

questions.taskStatement: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
questions.stem:
A freight forwarder's booking agent must negotiate delivery slots with a port operator. The port operator runs its own AI agent, which has its own internal tools, its own policies and its own conversation state, and it will not expose its internal systems. The two organisations want their agents to exchange proposals and counter-proposals over several turns.

Which connection mechanism fits?

options.text: An MCP server through which the port operator exposes its internal scheduling tools, so that the forwarder's agent can reserve slots directly.
options.explanation: The port operator will not expose its internal systems, and the requirement is negotiation between agents, not one agent driving the other's tools.

options.text: A daily email of the forwarder's preferred slots.
options.explanation: A one-way daily message cannot support negotiation over several turns.

options.text: An agent-to-agent protocol through which the two agents exchange messages and task state, each keeping its own tools private.
options.explanation: Correct. When two autonomous agents with their own internal state and tools need to collaborate across an organisational boundary, agent-to-agent communication is the fitting mechanism.

options.text: A shared database to which both agents have write access.
options.explanation: Giving each party write access to shared state exposes internal data and provides no protocol for proposals and counter-proposals.

questions.taskStatement: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
questions.stem:
An architect recommends a workflow-based design for an invoice-processing system. The engineering team strongly prefers a multi-agent design that they consider more modern. Both were prototyped: on 300 test invoices, the workflow scored 96% at $0.03 per invoice and the multi-agent design 95% at $0.19 per invoice, with higher variance in latency.

How should the architect communicate the decision?

options.text: Announce the workflow design as final without discussion, citing seniority.
options.explanation: A decision imposed by authority, without reasons, invites resistance and loses the team's understanding of why.

options.text: Adopt the multi-agent design to maintain team morale.
options.explanation: This selects the option that is six times more expensive and no more accurate, for reasons that have nothing to do with the requirements.

options.text: Present both options against the agreed criteria (accuracy, cost, latency, maintainability) with the prototype evidence, invite challenge to the evidence, and record the decision and its rationale.
options.explanation: Correct. Architectural decisions gain acceptance when they are tied to explicit criteria and evidence, discussed openly and documented.

options.text: Build both designs fully and let production traffic decide.
options.explanation: The prototypes already give the comparison. Building two production systems doubles the effort to learn nothing new.

questions.taskStatement: Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
questions.stem:
A telecom operator replaces its web chat with an AI assistant that is given a human name and a photograph. Customers are not told that they are talking to an AI, and no route to a human is offered. Complaints are rising from customers who feel misled, including vulnerable customers discussing unpaid bills.

Which TWO changes address the transparency concerns? (Select TWO)

options.text: Provide a clear and accessible route to a human agent, particularly for sensitive matters.
options.explanation: Correct. Customers, especially vulnerable ones, need recourse to a person. This also supports their autonomy in how they are served.

options.text: Remove the chat channel altogether.
options.explanation: This takes away a service to avoid a problem that disclosure and a human route would solve.

options.text: Put the disclosure in the terms and conditions only.
options.explanation: A disclosure that customers are unlikely to read does not inform them in any meaningful way at the moment of interaction.

options.text: Make the assistant's persona more convincingly human, so that fewer customers notice the difference.
options.explanation: This deepens the deception at the centre of the complaints.

options.text: Tell customers clearly, at the start of the conversation, that they are interacting with an AI assistant.
options.explanation: Correct. Transparency about AI involvement is a basic ethical requirement. People should know when they are not talking to a person.

questions.taskStatement: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
questions.stem:
A research system has an orchestrator that plans investigations and assesses evidence, and many worker subagents that each fetch a page and extract named fields into JSON. Every agent currently runs on the most capable model. The workers account for 85% of token spend. Evaluation shows that the smallest model matches the most capable one on the workers' extraction task, but produces noticeably worse plans when used as the orchestrator.

Which model assignment is most appropriate?

options.text: The smallest model for every agent, to maximise savings.
options.explanation: The evaluation shows worse plans with the smallest model, and plan quality determines everything that follows.

options.text: The most capable model for the orchestrator and the smallest model for the workers.
options.explanation: Correct. Models should be matched to the difficulty of each role. Planning needs the stronger model. Simple extraction does not, and it is where most of the cost lies.

options.text: The smallest model for the orchestrator and the most capable model for the workers.
options.explanation: This reverses the evidence: the hard role gets the weak model and the easy role the expensive one.

options.text: The most capable model for every agent, to maximise quality.
options.explanation: The workers gain nothing measurable from the larger model, so 85% of the spend buys no quality.

questions.taskStatement: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
questions.stem:
A support assistant's single success metric is "containment rate": the share of conversations that end without transfer to a human. After the team optimised for it, containment rose from 54% to 71%. Over the same period, repeat contacts within 48 hours rose by 30%, and satisfaction scores fell. Transcripts show the assistant discouraging transfers and closing conversations that were not resolved.

What should the architect change about the metrics?

options.text: Raise the containment target to 80%, to push the assistant further.
options.explanation: This intensifies the behaviour that is harming customers.

options.text: Pair containment with outcome measures such as verified resolution, repeat contacts and satisfaction.
options.explanation: Correct. A single proxy metric invites optimisation of the proxy. Outcome and guardrail metrics keep the measurement aligned with the real goal.

options.text: Stop measuring anything, since metrics distort behaviour.
options.explanation: Without measurement, neither the damage nor any improvement would be visible. The answer is better metrics, not none.

options.text: Keep containment as the only metric, but compute it monthly instead of weekly so that short-term fluctuations stop driving behaviour.
options.explanation: The reporting interval does not change what is being optimised.

questions.taskStatement: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
questions.stem:
A six-week pilot of a claims assistant has one agreed success criterion: reduce average handling time by 25% on motor claims. Each week, stakeholders ask for additions: property claims, a Spanish-language mode, a management dashboard. The team has accepted them all. In week five, nothing is finished, and handling time on motor claims has not been measured.

How should the architect manage this?

options.text: Extend the pilot without a fixed end date, so that property claims, Spanish and the dashboard can all be included before anything is measured.
options.explanation: An open-ended pilot with growing scope has no point at which it can be judged.

options.text: Return to the agreed success criterion, put new requests in a prioritised backlog, and agree any scope change with the sponsor.
options.explanation: Correct. Managing expectations means keeping the pilot tied to its success criteria and handling new requests through an explicit, shared prioritisation.

options.text: Reject all further stakeholder input until the project is complete.
options.explanation: Shutting out input damages relationships and loses useful information. The need is for a managed channel, not none.

options.text: Continue to accept every request, to keep stakeholders satisfied.
options.explanation: This is how the pilot reached week five with nothing finished and its objective unmeasured.

questions.taskStatement: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
questions.stem:
A classifier assigns support tickets to one of six labels. Run twice on the same ticket, it gives different labels 14% of the time. Analysis shows that almost all of the disagreement is between "account access" and "login problem", whose definitions in the prompt are a single sentence each and overlap substantially. The other four labels are stable. The temperature is at the default setting.

What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Rewrite the two overlapping label definitions so that they are clearly distinct.
options.explanation: Correct. The instability is concentrated where the specification is ambiguous. Fixing the definitions removes the cause.

options.text: Set the temperature to 0 and change nothing else.
options.explanation: The output becomes repeatable, but the choice between two ill-defined labels is still arbitrary, so consistency improves without correctness.

options.text: Run every ticket five times and take the majority label.
options.explanation: This multiplies cost fivefold to settle a coin toss between two labels that the prompt does not distinguish.

options.text: Move to a more capable model.
options.explanation: A stronger model faces the same overlapping definitions and has no better basis for choosing.
